        return None
    current = sum(values[:k])

        current += values[i] - values[i - k]

stratified_sample.tutor_response: That's exactly right, and your reading of the traceback is spot on. The key mechanism is that scope in Python is decided at compile time, not line by line: if a name is bound anywhere in a function — by assignment, by a `for` target, or by being a parameter — the compiler marks it local for the entire body, and every lookup of that name inside the function goes straight to the local slot. It never falls back to builtins just because the local happens to hold something uncallable. So both of your failures were the same defect wearing two costumes. With no argument the local held None, hence 'NoneType' object is not callable. With an argument it held your one-parameter callback, and the call site handed it a function and an iterable because that's the signature of the builtin you thought you were invoking, hence 'takes 1 positional argument but 2 were given' pointing at a lambda that was indeed yours, just being invoked by machinery you never intended. That's also why the traceback felt so disorienting: the frame that raised was your lambda, but the caller was the tail line, not the loop. This trap is much nastier for parameters than for module-level assignments, because a module-level rebinding at least only affects lookups that happen after it runs, whereas a parameter poisons the name from the first line of the function. It's worth knowing that `filter`, `list`, `type`, `id`, `input`, `format`, and `next` are the usual casualties, since they read so naturally as argument names; flake8-builtins (the A002 check) or a Ruff rule will flag exactly this if you want a mechanical guard. Nice bit of debugging.
